meta.title: Who really said "Every Ambitious Would-Be Empire Clarions It Abroad That She Is Conquering the World to Bring It Peace"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Thoreau. The passage was written by novelist Taylor Caldwell in her 1968 book Testimony of Two Men, where a character credits it to George S. Boutwell.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Every Ambitious Would-Be Empire Clarions It Abroad That She Is Conquering the World to Bring It Peace'?
meta.ogDescription: Written by Taylor Caldwell in a 1968 novel and put in a character’s mouth. Not Thoreau, and no evidence Boutwell said it either.

answer.label: Not Henry David Thoreau — Taylor Caldwell wrote it in a 1968 novel
answer.sourceLine: The passage appears in Taylor Caldwell’s 1968 novel Testimony of Two Men, where a character recalls the anti-imperialist politician George S. Boutwell saying it. Quote Investigator, whose earliest located citation this is, states that the words about empire were not written by Thoreau, has found no substantive support for the Boutwell ascription, and suggests Caldwell should be credited.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 1968, Doubleday & Company, Garden City, New York — quote page 452
Spoken by a character, who attributes it to George S. Boutwell

source.excerpt: Every ambitious would-be empire clarions it abroad that she is conquering the world to bring it peace, security and freedom, and is sacrificing her sons only for the most noble and humanitarian purposes. That is a lie, and it is an ancient lie, yet generations still rise and believe it!
trail: Quote Investigator’s earliest located instance is Taylor Caldwell’s Testimony of Two Men (1968), quote page 452, verified with scans. The words are dialogue, not narration the 1968 citation ↗.

The same speech in the novel embeds a second quotation, this one attributed to Thoreau — and that is where the Thoreau association comes from. Caldwell’s character renders it ‘If I knew a man was approaching my house to do me good, I would flee for my life’ the passage in full ↗.

That embedded line is genuinely Thoreau, but paraphrased. Walden reads ‘If I knew for a certainty that a man was coming to my house with the conscious design of doing me good, I should run for my life’ — confirmed in the full text Walden at Project Gutenberg ↗. The empire sentence is not in Walden.
The attribution to Thoreau was in public circulation by 2003, when the El Paso Times published a letter to the editor quoting the empire passage as his the 2003 letter ↗.
source.cutTag: Taylor Caldwell, Testimony of Two Men, 1968, page 452
source.excerptNote: The wording that circulates online is usually shortened — most often dropping ‘security and’ and cutting off before ‘That is a lie’. In the novel the sentence is dialogue: a character quoting, from memory and with an explicit hedge (‘if I am repeating him correctly’), a politician who died in 1905.

source.rightsHolder: The estate of Taylor Caldwell; first published by Doubleday & Company (1968)
source.rightsNote: In copyright. Testimony of Two Men was first published in 1968, well after the 1930 cut-off for the United States public domain, so the passage belongs to Caldwell’s estate and her publisher. Quote it as short comment or criticism with attribution rather than reproducing it at length. Note also that crediting it to Thoreau does not make it free to use — the words are still Caldwell’s. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Taylor Caldwell
author.heading: About Taylor Caldwell
author.metaLine: 1900–1985 · British-born American novelist of popular historical fiction
author.bio: Taylor Caldwell — born Janet Miriam Caldwell — produced bestsellers across four decades, several of them sprawling historical novels with strong political convictions running through them. Testimony of Two Men (1968) was popular enough to be adapted as a television miniseries in the 1970s, which is a large part of why a line of her dialogue escaped the book and went looking for a more famous author.

misattribution.heading: Three names, one novelist
misattribution.intro: This passage has been credited to three different people, and the reason is visible in the novel itself: Caldwell wrote a character quoting a politician, and embedded a real Thoreau paraphrase in the same speech.

items.why: Quote Investigator states directly that ‘the words about empire were not written by Henry David Thoreau’. The passage is absent from Walden search the full text ↗, and Caldwell’s 1968 novel remains the earliest known appearance.

items.who: A second, genuine Thoreau quote in the same speech
items.why: Caldwell’s character quotes Thoreau’s ‘doing me good’ line immediately before the empire sentence. Two quotations, one paragraph — and the attribution slid from the first onto the second the passage ↗.

The novel’s character credits Boutwell, but Quote Investigator has found no substantive evidence he said or wrote it, and notes Caldwell demonstrably paraphrased the Thoreau line in the same breath — so she may well have paraphrased Boutwell too QI’s reasoning ↗.
It is her sentence, on her page, in her novel. Everything downstream is a quotation of Caldwell the conclusion ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Written by Taylor Caldwell in Testimony of Two Men (1968, p. 452) and spoken by a fictional character — not by Thoreau, and with no evidence for Boutwell the evidence ↗.

context.heading: Why it travels
lead: The sentence is built to be quoted: a general law about empires, a flat verdict (‘That is a lie’), and a closing turn about each generation falling for it again. It reads like something written in 1849 by a man in a cabin, which is exactly why Thoreau’s name fits it so comfortably.

It was in fact written in 1968, at the height of American argument over Vietnam, by a popular novelist putting words into the mouth of a nineteenth-century anti-imperialist. The anachronism is the point of the effect — and the reason the quotation lost its author.
detailsBody: Caldwell’s character introduces the speech with an explicit hedge — ‘if I am repeating him correctly’ — which is a novelist signalling that this is a recollection, not a transcript. Quote Investigator picks up on exactly that: because the Thoreau line in the same passage is demonstrably altered, an electronic search for a matching Boutwell original may be futile even if one exists.

The lesson is a general one for quotation hunting. A line spoken by a fictional character, attributed inside the fiction to a real person, is one of the most reliable ways for a sentence to escape its author — the quotation marks travel, the novel does not.
